topic: Multi-intent task decomposition for LLM tool and skill routing
name: Voyager / ReAct variants
description: A family of agent-loop execution models in which task decomposition is implicit in the LLM's chain-of-thought rather than produced by an explicit splitter node. The canonical baseline is ReAct (Yao et al., arXiv:2210.03629, ICLR 2023), which interleaves Reason -> Act -> Observe steps so that the model selects one tool per turn and re-plans turn-by-turn from each new observation. Voyager (Wang et al., arXiv:2305.16291, NVIDIA/Caltech, 2023) extends the loop into a lifelong-learning embodied agent in Minecraft with three pieces: an automatic curriculum (LLM proposes the next task), an ever-growing skill library of executable JavaScript functions indexed by embeddings of their NL descriptions, and an iterative prompting mechanism that refines code using environment feedback, execution errors, and a GPT-4 self-verifier. Related variants include Reflexion (verbal self-critique + episodic memory), ReWOO (plan-all-tools-upfront, observation-free), and AutoGPT-style autonomous loops. Across all of these, routing happens implicitly via per-turn tool/skill selection, not via a dedicated decomposition+dispatch planner.
decomposition_method: LLM-prompted (zero-shot / few-shot CoT), implicit. There is no separate splitter: the model's chain-of-thought decides the next sub-action turn-by-turn. In ReAct the 'Thought' step implicitly decomposes the task one action at a time; in Voyager an automatic-curriculum GPT-4 prompt proposes the next task given agent state/inventory/completed+failed tasks (CoT prompting), and a separate action-generation prompt writes code for it. No fine-tuned splitter, parser, or grammar; decomposition is emergent from the prompted LLM. (Voyager's curriculum is closer to skill-tree/curriculum traversal than a one-shot split.)
decomposition_granularity: tool call (ReAct: one action/tool per turn) to milestone+steps (Voyager: the curriculum proposes a milestone-level task, e.g. 'craft a stone pickaxe', which the iterative-prompting loop realizes as a multi-step executable skill/program). So granularity ranges from single tool call (ReAct/Reflexion) to milestone-with-internal-steps (Voyager skills).
ordering_strategy: dynamic (mid-chain re-plan). Ordering is decided incrementally: each turn's reasoning conditions on the latest observation, so the agent re-plans continuously rather than committing to a DAG upfront. Voyager's automatic curriculum sequences tasks adaptively (bottom-up, matched to current capability). ReWOO (a variant) is the exception: it is fixed sequential / plan-upfront with no per-step re-planning. No topological DAG or parallel fan-out in the core ReAct/Voyager loop.
decomposition_validation: Mostly none / blind trust in the per-turn LLM reasoning, with one notable exception: Voyager adds a self-verification module (a separate GPT-4 acting as a critic) that checks whether a proposed/executed task actually succeeded before the skill is committed to the library, and the iterative-prompting loop runs up to ~4 refinement rounds using execution errors and environment feedback. This is outcome verification of a single skill, not a pre-dispatch check of a full decomposition's solvability/completeness/non-redundancy (contrast AOP's detector + reward model). ReAct and Reflexion have no decomposition validator at all; Reflexion only adds post-hoc verbal self-critique after a trajectory. [uncertain]
hierarchy_depth: flat for ReAct/Reflexion/ReWOO (a single running loop of sub-actions, no nested sub-agents). Voyager is effectively two-level: an automatic-curriculum layer that proposes milestone tasks above an action/skill layer that realizes each as a multi-step program, plus a growing skill library that composes earlier skills into later ones (compositional, but not a fixed milestone->step tree). [uncertain]
router_type: chain / sequential elimination via in-context tool selection. Routing is not a classifier over a full DAG; at each turn the LLM picks the next tool/skill from the available set in-context (ReAct). Voyager adds retrieve-then-(implicit-)rerank: the top-5 skills most relevant to the current task are fetched from the skill library by embedding similarity and injected into the prompt, and the LLM selects/composes among them. So: per-turn in-context selection (ReAct) plus embedding retrieval of candidate skills (Voyager).
routing_model: prompted LLM (same model as the main agent; GPT-3.5/GPT-4/LLaMA for ReAct, GPT-4 for Voyager). No separate fine-tuned router or RL-trained router. Voyager adds an embedding-similarity component (skill descriptions embedded for top-k retrieval), making it a hybrid of prompted-LLM selection + embedding retrieval. Candidate gating in Voyager is otherwise rule-free beyond embedding rank.
handles_ambiguity: best-effort pick / overconfident-allow. At each turn the LLM commits to the single tool/skill its reasoning favors; there is no clarification request to the user, no abstain, and no explicit uncertainty model (no POMDP). Ambiguity or a wrong choice is handled reactively: the next observation may contradict the action and the loop re-reasons (ReAct), Voyager's self-verifier may reject the result and trigger another refinement round, and Reflexion stores a verbal lesson for the retry. This is recovery-after-the-fact, not principled ambiguity resolution. [uncertain]
fallback_behavior: retry / re-plan within the loop (route to general LLM reasoning). When no skill/tool fits or an action fails, the agent does not abort or escalate to a human; it loops: ReAct re-reasons from the error observation; Voyager's iterative prompting feeds execution errors + self-verification feedback back into the action-generation prompt for up to ~4 rounds, and the curriculum can defer/replace the task; Reflexion writes a self-reflection and retries. Persistent failure simply yields a degraded final answer or task abandonment after an iteration cap (no formal human-escalation node). [uncertain]
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: ReAct: full-context (all tool definitions placed in the prompt) — does not scale beyond a small toolset. Voyager directly addresses scale: skills are stored in a vector DB and retrieved top-5 by embedding similarity of the query/task against skill descriptions, so only relevant skills enter the prompt as the library grows (lifelong accumulation). This is embedding retrieval (top-k) rather than two-stage rerank or skill-tree traversal. Voyager's compositional skills also reduce prompt pressure by packaging multi-step behavior into one callable function. [uncertain]
router_agent_asymmetry: Low / none. The same LLM both routes (selects/composes the skill in-context) and executes the reasoning; the routing prompt and the agent prompt see the same skill information (retrieved skill code + descriptions in Voyager). There is no deliberate router-vs-agent information asymmetry as later formalized by SkillRouter. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: ReAct loop (implicit, one tool at a time). The defining trait of this family: a sequential agent loop where each turn issues at most one action, observes, and re-reasons. Voyager runs the same loop but each action can be a composite skill (a multi-step program) executed atomically in the environment. ReWOO is the variant that batches all tool calls after a single planning pass (closer to parallel fan-out), but core ReAct/Voyager are strictly one-action-per-turn sequential.
parallel_vs_concurrent: Neither, in the core loop — ReAct/Voyager execute one action per turn (fully sequential), a recognized structural limitation: the loop precludes parallel execution of independent operations and incurs a new LLM inference per observation. The ReWOO variant enables parallel tool execution (all planned tools run together, then a single solver synthesizes), and ablations (e.g., GAIA2 Parallel-Tool-Calling) show large latency/token savings vs. the ReAct scaffold, but that is a departure from the canonical single-tool-per-turn pattern. [uncertain]
dependency_detection: assumed-sequential (implicit). Dependencies are never declared; each turn just consumes the running observation history, so ordering/dependency emerges from the LLM's reasoning rather than an explicit DAG or learned classifier. The loop conservatively treats everything as sequential (each action may depend on the prior observation). ReWOO is the exception — its planner emits placeholder variables to express which tool outputs feed which later calls, allowing independent ones to run in parallel.
result_aggregation: iterative (each result feeds the next prompt). There is no separate joiner: the running scratchpad/observation history accumulates and the LLM's final turn produces the answer from that context. Voyager additionally aggregates by committing verified skills to the library for reuse (cross-task accumulation) and composing them into later skills. ReWOO has an explicit final 'Solver' that reads all collected tool outputs at once (closer to an LLM joiner). [uncertain]
mid_chain_feedback: hard. This family's signature is continuous re-planning: every observation can change the next action (ReAct), Voyager's self-verifier/error feedback drives explicit re-attempts and curriculum adjustment, and Reflexion injects verbal critiques into the next attempt. Later steps fully use earlier results to re-route; the plan is never locked upfront (except in the ReWOO variant, which is the opposite extreme: no mid-chain feedback).
benchmark_name: ReAct: HotpotQA, FEVER (knowledge tasks); ALFWorld, WebShop (interactive decision-making). Voyager: MineDojo/Minecraft, evaluated on tech-tree milestone unlock speed, number of unique items discovered (63 across 160 iterations), map exploration, and zero-shot transfer to a fresh world. Reflexion: HumanEval, ALFWorld, HotpotQA. ReWOO: HotpotQA, TriviaQA, GSM8K, etc. Newer ablations use GAIA2 to compare ReAct vs parallel-tool-calling scaffolds.
multi_intent_coverage: Partial / implicit. These benchmarks are long-horizon sequential-decision tasks (dependent sub-tasks discovered on the fly) rather than explicitly labeled parallel/multiple/parallel_multiple compound prompts (as in BFCL v3). Voyager's open-ended Minecraft tasks are sequential and compositional (later goals depend on earlier-acquired skills); ALFWorld/WebShop are sequential. So multi-intent is covered as sequential/dependent decomposition, not as benchmark-tagged parallel independent intents.
accuracy_metric: outcome-based, task-specific. ReAct: exact-match QA accuracy (HotpotQA), label accuracy (FEVER), task success rate (ALFWorld/WebShop). Voyager: state-based / environment outcomes — tech-tree milestones reached, unique items obtained, distance traveled, zero-shot task completion (world-state after execution). Reflexion: pass@1 (HumanEval), success rate (ALFWorld). Generally final-outcome / world-state oriented rather than per-step process supervision.
clarification_capability: None. ReAct/Voyager/Reflexion never ask the user clarifying questions and are not evaluated on when-to-ask vs. when-to-answer; ReAct's only human interaction is optional human-in-the-loop thought-editing (a person rewrites a 'Thought' to steer the agent), not agent-initiated clarification. These systems exemplify the overconfident-answer pattern later quantified by InteractComp/ClarifyBench. [uncertain]
process_vs_outcome_eval: Predominantly outcome-only (final answer / task success / world-state). ReAct does emphasize interpretable intermediate traces, and Voyager's self-verifier scores intermediate skill success, but headline metrics are outcome-based; there is no learned process-reward model scoring each decomposition step. [uncertain]
eval_stability: Low / live-environment dependent. ReAct uses a live Wikipedia API and live interactive environments; Voyager runs against a live Minecraft (MineDojo) instance and live GPT-4, so numbers are sensitive to model/API drift and environment stochasticity. No cached/virtual API server (unlike StableToolBench). Voyager reports averages over multiple seeds to mitigate variance. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: in-context (prompted) agent loop, implemented as a standalone harness. ReAct is a prompting pattern around a single LLM with a tool interface; Voyager is an open-source standalone system (curriculum prompt + action-generation prompt + self-verifier + vector skill library + Minecraft/Mineflayer bot interface). Widely re-implemented as a node/loop in agent frameworks (LangChain/LangGraph ReAct agents). Not an inference-engine-layer or middleware router; orchestration lives in the application layer via prompts.
routing_layer: application-layer. All tool/skill selection happens in-context at the application/agent layer via LLM prompting; nothing is pushed into an inference-engine or proxy layer.
latency_overhead: High per-trajectory because routing is amortized over many turns: each ReAct turn costs a full LLM inference, and latency/token cost grow with trajectory length (a recognized ReAct weakness for predictable workflows). There is no separate upfront decomposition call (decomposition is folded into each turn), but Voyager adds extra calls per task: curriculum proposal + action generation + self-verification + up to ~4 refinement rounds + embedding retrieval, making each Voyager task several LLM calls. ReWOO is the low-overhead variant (2 LLM calls total, ~5x token efficiency vs ReAct). [uncertain]
online_adaptation: ReAct/Reflexion: static at deploy for parameters (no weight updates), though Reflexion adapts within an episode/across retries via an episodic memory of verbal reflections, and Voyager performs in-context lifelong learning — its skill library grows from production experience and is reused across tasks/worlds without any fine-tuning. So Voyager is adaptive via a non-parametric (skill-library + embedding) memory rather than via RL/bandit or SFT-from-logs. No gradient-based router learning. [uncertain]
adoption: Open-source (with code), research-grade. ReAct (code + widely adopted as the default agent pattern in LangChain/LlamaIndex/LangGraph and most agent frameworks). Voyager open-sourced at github.com/MineDojo/Voyager with project site voyager.minedojo.org; influential reference for skill-library/lifelong-agent designs. Reflexion and ReWOO also open-source. No single commercial product, but the ReAct loop underpins many production agents.
